items.title: Self-service kiosks at a leading hospital
items.result: 178 patient interviews, 94 usability tests and 489 heuristic findings in seven weeks: why kiosks rated positively by 87% of patients still needed a concierge standing next to them.

items.title: Marketing analytics platform
items.result: The client asked how to grow adoption of the marketing data platform by 30%. Research showed the problem wasn't only the dashboards: a heuristic review, 11 usability tests and 22 flowcharts became 13 ideas and a 3-to-5-year roadmap.

items.title: Shotlist
items.result: An inherited production-planning platform with 34 open bugs and half-built features: first we diagnosed and stabilized it, then redesigned it in three layers, from the quick shotlist to the agency workspace.

items.title: Designing for an AI-operated platform
items.result: How a designer governs what the product's AI may say and render: a two-layer widget contract, response guidelines and the wizard that connects external agents to the platform.

items.title: Inheritance instead of copies
items.result: Letting an offer diverge from its product without duplicating the product or migrating data: three incompatible mechanisms found in the code became one resolver, three states and seven guard-rails, handed off as 18 issues.
items.scope: Systems design, data model, API spec, executable prototype

items.title: Monetization foundation
items.result: Where plan, credit and wallet live in a multi-workspace platform, and how a free tier that blocked creation became "create freely, gating happens at publish".

about.p1: I've been a product designer for over ten years, mostly in B2B and in domains where mistakes are expensive: banking, insurance, SaaS billing. I started in graphic design as a teenager, went through nearly 4,000 hours of technical training for WorldSkills, and came back as an instructor before moving into digital product.
about.p2: Today I own product design for a B2B all-in-one platform: I design its embedded AI assistant, rebuilt the design system on a single token source that feeds Figma, code and what the AI renders, and use AI to carry prototypes into the product's codebase, where developers take over.
about.p3: I led teams for over four years. I like managing. I'd rather build.

method.title: How I work
method.lede: I do not write code. I design product and work with AI to carry the design into code, as close as possible to where it will live. This page explains the method behind the cases.

sections.label: Starting point
sections.title: Architects, not bricklayers
paragraphs: Every workstream goes through a short shaping cycle: a brief that defines the problem and the appetite, a frame that settles the solution in broad strokes, and a package engineering can build without asking me what I meant. The team's rule is that we design the whole house before laying the first brick, and we only lay bricks once everyone has seen the plan.
What changes with AI is how fast the plan becomes something you can walk through.

sections.label: Rule one
sections.title: Every claim about code is read at the source
paragraphs: Before proposing, I read the repository with the help of a coding assistant: what exists, how it works, what has been tried. I do not trust a meeting summary to know how the system behaves. That is how I found three incompatible mechanisms where the request saw one, and no per-plan permission where everyone assumed there was one.
It changes the conversation with engineering: I arrive with what exists, not with what I imagine exists.

sections.label: Rule two
sections.title: Nothing goes into a package without a complete prototype
paragraphs: The exit gate of shaping is a self-contained HTML prototype: one file, opens in any browser, with every screen and state of the workstream. When the logic matters, the prototype runs the logic, like the inheritance resolver engineering later implemented in four lines.
The prototype is written with AI from the design and the rules. I decide what it does; the AI writes how.
evidence: screens in 7 prototypes of one workstream
lines to prove a business rule

sections.label: Rule three
sections.title: Big things are born in Figma, small things are born in code
paragraphs: The design system is built in Figma with AI operating the file through MCP: variables are born from the token file, dark mode is generated by automation, components are ported bottom-up. A color picker that took an hour and a half in code came out in seconds in Figma; a token adjustment that would open dozens of components is one line in the file.
Knowing where each decision costs less is half the job.
evidence: Figma variables generated from one file
dark mode values generated, none missing
source of truth for Figma, code and AI

sections.label: Rule four
sections.title: The design goes all the way to the product's code
paragraphs: Once a workstream is settled, I use AI to carry the prototype into the product's repository, as draft code changes that developers take over, review and finish. The process was defined together with engineering: concept prototype, changes in phases, design review at the end.
I do not open a code editor to write. I open it to read, compare and approve. The credit for the code that ships belongs to the engineering team; mine is for the design arriving there whole.

sections.label: Rule five
sections.title: Every decision is recorded
paragraphs: I keep a system of notes in which every workstream has context, decisions, constraints and open items, and every case in this portfolio was born from it. The AI reads that context before any task; I reread it before any meeting. It is what lets a package of 30 tasks become 18 coherent issues rather than a pile of loose requests.

sections.label: What AI does not do
sections.title: Decide, listen and go into the field
paragraphs: AI does not decide what the product should do, does not talk to the client, does not interview patients in a hospital and does not notice the queue forming next to a kiosk. All of that is still the work, and it is the part I like most.

What it does is shorten the distance between the decision and the proof. This site is an example: it was designed by me and built as a human + AI collaboration, and the code is public in the repository.
